nameStory: The 'sinewed' in this lichen's name refers to its tough, stringy branches that resemble the fibrous tendons that connect muscles to bones. When you handle a clump of this bushy lichen, you can feel how the individual branches have that wiry, tendon-like strength that won't easily break or crumble.
description: Sinewed Bushy Lichen is a pale green, shrubby lichen that grows in tangled clusters from tree bark and rocks. This fruticose (shrub-like) lichen forms dense tufts of narrow, branching strands that look almost like tiny green coral. The whole clump can grow several inches across, with individual branches reaching 1-3 inches long. Its pale green color can appear almost whitish when dry and becomes more vibrant when wet.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms dense, tangled tufts of narrow, repeatedly branching strands that feel tough and wiry to the touch, like fine green wire or dried seaweed

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale green to grayish-green when dry, becoming more vibrant green when moistened by rain or fog

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Branches have tiny white pores called pseudocyphellae that look like small holes or breaks in the surface when viewed closely

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Grows on tree bark, especially hardwoods, and occasionally on rocks in areas with good air quality

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: May produce small, disk-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) at branch tips, though these are not always present

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual tufts typically 1-4 inches across, with branches 1-3 inches long that divide into progressively finer segments

habitat: Look for Sinewed Bushy Lichen on the bark of hardwood trees like oaks and maples, particularly in areas with clean air and moderate humidity. It's most common in coastal and near-coastal regions of New England where sea fog provides regular moisture. This species indicates good air quality and is less common in urban areas with heavy pollution.

seasonality.spring: Bright green and plump from spring rains, making it easy to spot against dark tree bark. This is an excellent time to observe the contrast between wet and dry coloration.
seasonality.summer: May appear more pale and brittle during dry spells, but becomes vibrant green again after summer thunderstorms or in foggy conditions.
seasonality.fall: Remains visible as leaves drop, often appearing more prominent on bare branches. Fall rains can make it particularly lush and colorful.
seasonality.winter: Persists through winter snows, often appearing grayish-white when dry but turning green when moistened by melting snow or winter rains.

funFact: This lichen can actually 'drink' water directly from fog through its branches, making it perfectly adapted to New England's coastal climate where morning fog rolls in from the ocean and provides moisture even during dry periods.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bushy lichens in the same genus, but Sinewed Bushy Lichen's tough, wiry texture and small surface pores (pseudocyphellae) help distinguish it. Memory trick: 'Sinewed' feels strong like a sinew - if the branches break easily when dry, it's probably a different species.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'Ramalina' comes from the Latin word for 'little branch,' referring to the branching growth pattern shared by all lichens in this genus. Despite being called 'bushy lichens,' these are quite different from true bushes - they're actually a partnership between fungi and algae.
compareHints: Compared to other Ramalina species in New England, Sinewed Bushy Lichen has straighter spores and more pronounced pseudocyphellae than Rock Bushy Lichen. It's typically more robust and wiry than the flatter, ribbon-like Frayed Ribbon Lichen, and lacks the powdery surface coating found on Farinose Cartilage Lichen.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rock Bushy Lichen is typically smaller and more exclusively rock-dwelling than its relatives like Sinewed Bushy Lichen, which prefers tree bark.
Unlike its relatives in the bushy lichen genus, Frayed Ribbon Lichen has distinctly split and frayed branch tips rather than smooth or merely pointed ends.
